title: Canada wants the EU to step up as a global power. Does Europe?
text:
Canada wants the EU to step up as a global power. Does Europe?
The European Union has given Prime Minister Mark Carney a warm welcome, but whether it goes big with its offer of associate membership for Canada is unclear.
In his bid to dramatically tighten transatlantic ties, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking an economic lifeline for his country. But perhaps more important, he is throwing down a challenge to Europe.
Canada needs friends to weather its trade war with the United States. But in addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, he laid out in urgent terms Canada’s need for allies that share its values on the international stage.
He left no doubt of what he thinks Canada and the European Union can accomplish together. In a time of global disruption and great-power politics, the alliance would be a “beacon for democracies” that could “help to create the next just, stable, and prosperous world order.”
With President Donald Trump engaging in a trade war against Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney is turning across the Atlantic for partners. The European Union has welcomed him, but will it take the unprecedented step of drawing Canada into its orbit?
“We do not seek power to dominate others,” he added. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one, no one, can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
The question is whether the EU will accept that charge.
Historically, it is not accustomed to thinking this way. It has often been less a leader than a mediator among 27 fractious member states, finding success in each incremental step.
But in inviting Canada to become an associate member, EU leadership is clearly trying to rattle the continent’s bureaucratic cages. Perhaps less important than the narrow question of what Canada’s associate membership might entail is a new vision of what the EU can be.
“The dilemma is that the EU is so used to thinking in legalistic terms: You’re in, or you’re out,” says Anand Sundar, special adviser to the director at the European Council on Foreign Relations. “Can it use this opportunity to boost its influence in the world and become a geopolitical actor, or is it going to return to its nitpicking and waste this opportunity?”
The “associate member” mystery
What an “associate member” might be, no one has any idea. Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, appears to have largely invented the concept to lay down a marker of ambition. In her State of the European Union address Wednesday, she said Canada would be the “first,” suggesting a template for a new form of relationship with the broader world.
A robust deal with Canada would be a litmus test. “It would send a signal that the EU is serious about becoming tighter with like-minded partners ... that don’t want to fall in line with the U.S.,” says Zach Meyers, director of research for the Centre on Regulation in Europe, or CERRE, a think tank in Brussels that focuses on regulation.
For the EU, that is uncharted territory. On one hand, it has numerous and varied relationships with different nations around the world, including a free-trade deal with Canada itself. But those pacts take years, even decades, to craft. Ms. von der Leyen’s commitment to bringing “the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible” without any sense of what that might practically mean or how it will be done speaks to a determination to redefine the EU and its traditional ways of doing business almost by force.
Such a shift in mindset is in some ways just as important as any deal that comes from it, some observers say. “If they just devote their time to technical things, I don’t think that’s going to do it,” says Dave Keating, a journalist in Brussels and author of the Gulf Stream Blues Substack on transatlantic relations. “They need something that’s a big, bold alliance.”
There are signs that could happen. Jean-Louis De Brouwer of the Brussels-based Egmont Institute recently sat in on a senior-level meeting among European and Canadian officials. He was struck by the tone. Amid so much gloom in Europe over areas ranging from the economy to politics to security, the meeting “was refreshing and was bringing optimism,” says Mr. De Brouwer. Everyone left with a sense that deepening the relationship “was something worth doing,” he adds.
Canada’s pressing needs
From Canada’s perspective, it makes sense. Economically, no country is going to replace the U.S., where Canada has sent more than half its exports for at least three-quarters of a century. But by strengthening relationships with other partners, “Do you get to a point of diversification where the U.S. leverage over Canada’s economy is somewhat diminished?” asks Eric Miller, president of Rideau Potomac Strategy Group and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute. That’s the goal.
The EU’s appeal to Canada is about more than just dollars and cents, however. Canada has recently significantly ramped up its cooperation with Europe on defense. That shows where Canada’s deeper interests lie, says Achim Hurrelmann, co-director of the Centre for European Studies at Carleton University in Ottawa.
“That primarily has to do with values, a willingness to protect what remains of the NATO alliance and multilateral collaboration,” he says. “Canada and the EU, ... including the U.K., have found that they have similar perceptions of global issues from Ukraine to Gaza to the Iran war.”
An April 2025 YouGov poll found that 44% of Canadians favored becoming part of the EU. That is impossible, as membership is open only to European countries. But even trying to become an associate member could be hard enough.
Why an alliance might fizzle
Despite the current momentum, doubts remain. Ten EU countries haven’t even ratified the free-trade deal yet. In France, for example, farmers worry about Canadian competition. “Constituencies in Europe won’t care about the bigger geopolitical game,” says Mr. Meyers of CERRE. They will only care about how any alliance with Canada affects their livelihoods.
This has been the EU’s greatest weakness when it comes to projecting power in a new landscape dominated by the U.S. and China. Big ideas inevitably run into bickering among 27 nations. “There’s definitely not a consensus” around the relationship with Canada, says Mr. Meyers. Reports suggest many in the EU were taken aback by Ms. von der Leyen’s offer of associate membership. Mr. Carney has downplayed the designation.
Yet the match is a natural one on many levels. With its close ties to Britain and France, as well as its more liberal political mindset, Canada is probably the most European non-European country. And the EU has positioned itself as a leader in upholding the liberal values that shaped the West after World War II.
“The EU becomes more attractive as countries seek allies,” says Heather Grabbe, a senior fellow at Bruegel, an economic think tank in Brussels. “Trump, through his policies, is driving these allies to form clubs that do not include the U.S.”
